questions.q:
Three statements are given followed by three conclusions numbered I, II and III. Assuming the statements to be true, even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which of the conclusions logically follow(s) from the statements.

Statements:

Some spices are medicines.

All medicines are chemicals.

No chemical is cheap.

Conclusions:

I. Some medicines are cheap.

II. Some chemicals are spices.

III. No medicine is cheap.
options: Only conclusions I and III follow.
Only conclusions II and III follow.
Only conclusions I and II follow.
questions.solution:
Statements:

Some spices are medicines.

All medicines are chemicals.

No chemical is cheap.



Conclusions:

I. Some medicines are cheap → Does not follow → As all medicines are chemicals and no chemical is cheap. So some medicines are cheap is not definitely followed.

II. Some chemicals are spices → Follow → As some spices are medicines and all medicines are chemicals. So some chemicals are spices is definitely followed.

III. No medicine is cheap → Follow → As all medicines are chemicals and no chemical is cheap. So no medicine is cheap is definitely followed.

So, Only conclusions II and III follow.

Hence, the correct answer is "Option 2".

• Redox is a reaction in which oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously.

• The reaction in which the addition of oxygen or removal of hydrogen takes place is known as an oxidation reaction.

• Oxidation can also be defined in terms of loss of electrons.

• Magnesium is designated as Mg.

• Atomic no. of Mg is 12

• Thus oxidation of Mg occurs by losing 2 electrons, and Mg forms Mg+2 ions.

• When Mg ribbon is burnt in presence of oxygen it reacts with the elemental oxygen forming Magnesium oxide.

questions.q: What was the duration of Rolling Plan in India?
questions.solution:
Correct answer 1978 to 1980

Key Points:

• Rolling Plan in India was started in 1978.

• The rolling plan concept was coined by Gunnar Myrdal.

• This plan was rejected again by the Indian National Congress government when it came to power in 1980 and a new sixth plan was made.

• The main advantage of the rolling plans is that they are flexible.

• The Rolling Plan is a plan in which every year the performance of the plan is assessed and a new plan is made next year based on this assessment.

• Thus, both the allocation and targets are revised during this plan.

• In India, the Janta Government terminated the fifth five-year plan in 1977-78 and launched its own sixth five-year plan for the period 1978-83 and called it a Rolling Plan.

Additional Information:

​A brief summary of the 5-year plans are:

Five-year plan

Time Period

Comment

First Plan
1951-56
During the initial years of independence, the economy was facing the problem of large-scale foodgrains import (1951) and there was the pressure of price rise. In the plan, the highest priority was given to agriculture including irrigation and power projects.

Second Plan
1956-61
The plan period was 1956–61. The plan laid emphasis on rapid industrialization with a focus on heavy industries and capital goods. The architect of this plan was Professor Mahalanobis.

Third Plan
1961-65
This plan incorporated the development of agriculture as one of the objectives of planning in India. It also for the first time, considered the aim of balanced, regional development. Significant events like the war with China in 1961– 62 and with Pakistan in 1965–66 affected the performance of this plan. Also, severe drought-led famine in 1965–66 led to a heavy drain and diversion of funds, so this plan utterly failed to meet its targets.

Three annual plans
1966-69
The fourth plan was ready for implementation in 1966- still the government opted for three annual plans due to weak financial situation and low morale after the defeat by China. Experts, as well as the opposition, called this period as a discontinuity in the planning process. So they named it a period of “Plan Holiday”, i.e., a period when no planning was carried out.

Fourth Plan
1969-74
The Plan was based on the Gadgil strategy (named after Dhananjay Ramchandra Gadgil, who was a social scientist who had helped in determining the allocation of central assistance for state plans in India.). There was a focus on the ideas of growth with stability and progress towards self-reliance. This plan led to the beginning of the politicisation of planning in India. This led to frequent double-digit inflations, unchecked increase in the fiscal deficits etc. Also, there was a first move in the direction of ‘nationalisation’. Greater control and regulation of the economy were some of the salient features of this plan

Fifth Plan
1974-79
This plan had its focus on poverty alleviation and self-reliance. The popular rhetoric of poverty alleviation was sensationalised a lot to the extent that the then Indira Gandhi government came out with a fresh plan, i.e., the Twenty-point Programme (1975).

Twenty point programme gave little importance to the objective of ‘growth with stability’ (one of the major objectives of the Fourth Plan).

Twenty Point programme
1975

Sixth Plan
1980-85
Due to the draconian emergency, there was a change in the government at the centre. The new government cut-short the fifth plan by a year to the fiscal 1977–78 and came up with the sixth Plan for the period 1978–83 it was called the ‘Rolling Plan’

In 1980, again government changed at the Centre, Indira led congress came back and it abandoned the rolling plan and came up with a fresh sixth plan (1980-85). This Plan was launched with the slogan of ‘Garibi Hatao’ (alleviate poverty).

Seventh Plan
1985-90
This plan greatly emphasized on rapid foodgrain production, increased employment creation and productivity in general. The basis of planning, i.e., growth, self-reliance and social justice and modernization in this plan too were the guiding principles. In 1989 the government launched the Jawahar Rojgar Yojana (JRY) to create wage-employment for the rural poor.

Two annual Plans
1990-92

Due to the fast-changing political situation at the central level also due to the pathbreaking and restructuring-oriented suggestions which were there in the eighth plan, the eighth plan could not take off. The new government, which came in the power in 1991 decided to commence the Eighth Plan for the period 1992–97 and that the fiscals 1990–91 and 1991–92 were then decided as two separate annual plans.

Eighth Plan
1992-97
This was the first plan in the new economic environment after the opening of the economy. The economic reforms which began in 1991 led to structural adjustment and macro-stabilization policies. As the economy moved towards liberalization, there was also severe criticism directed at the move. The opinion was that as the country was now entering into the market economy zone and the state is ‘rolling back’, planning makes no sense.

Ninth Plan
1997-2002
This plan was launched when due to the South East Asian Financial Crisis in 1996-97, there was an all-round ‘slowdown’ in the economy. But by now the economy was almost out of the fiscal imbroglio of the early 1990s. The plan targeted an ambitious high growth rate of per cent and also aimed towards time-bound ‘social’ objectives. There was an emphasis on the seven identified Basic Minimum Services (BMS).

Tenth Plan
2002-07
The Plan mandated greater participation of the NDC in the formulation of planning. Some highly important steps like doubling of per capita income in 10 years; improving quality of life should also come with higher growth rates. Also, ‘Governance’ was considered a factor of development.

Eleventh Plan
2007-12
This plan targeted a growth rate of 10 per cent and also voiced the idea of ‘inclusive growth’.

Twelfth Plan
2012-17
This plan was prepared by the Planning Commission after the widest and most comprehensive consultation to date as the government believed that citizens are now better informed and literate and are also keen to engage. The plan aimed at a growth rate of 9 per cent. It also emphasized the need to intensify efforts to have a 4 per cent average growth in the agriculture sector.

Profit = ₹75

Additional Information

Marked Price (MP) & Discount

You must aware of friends who speak against you.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'beware of'.

Key Points

• The underlined part in the given sentence is grammatically incorrect.

• Here, 'beware of' should be used instead of 'aware of'.

• By using "beware of" instead of "you must aware of," the warning becomes more direct and urgent, as "beware" implies a sense of imminent danger or harm. Additionally, "beware of" is a common and idiomatic expression, while "you must aware of" is not typically used in English.

• The phrase "beware of" is a better fit in this sentence because it conveys a sense of caution or wariness towards someone or something that may pose a danger or threat. It is often used as a warning to others to be on the lookout for potential harm or trouble.

• *For example, if someone tells you to "beware of pickpockets" when you're traveling in a crowded city, it means you should be careful and watchful of your belongings so that you don't become a victim of theft.*

• So in the context of the given sentence, the correct phrase is *"beware of friends who speak against you,"* which means that you should be cautious and watchful of any friends who might be speaking negatively about you behind your back.

Correct Sentence: *You must beware of friends who speak against you.*

The good weather has been a boon for many businesses located near the beach.

The correct answer is 'beneficial'.

Key Points

• The most appropriate synonym of the given word 'boon' is 'beneficial'.

• *Example: The new vaccine is a boon for the health of the population.*

• Beneficial - लाभदायक - Producing good or helpful results or effects; advantageous.

• *Example: The new exercise routine has proven to be highly beneficial for her health.*

Correct Answer: *Beneficial.*

questions.q:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.

A. While India is home to 75 per cent of tigers in the world, the Global Tiger Day - as it is also known - sees awareness events organised in the country, as well as neighbouring Bangladesh and Nepal.

B. Its primary objective is to preserve the natural habitat of the tiger.

C. International Tiger Day was initiated in 2010, at the Saint Petersburg Tiger Summit.

D. This annual event, observed on 29 July, aims to create awareness on tiger conservation.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'CDBA'.

Key Points

• The given question is an example of a Para Jumble.

• We know that the first statement of a para jumbled question is usually an independent general statement, a noun, a universal fact, starting of an incident, or it starts with 'most' or 'once'.

• Sentence C begins by introducing the topic of International Tiger Day, which was initiated in 2010 at the Saint Petersburg Tiger Summit. This sentence provides the context for the remaining sentences and explains what the paragraph will be about.

• Sentence D then explains that International Tiger Day is observed annually on 29 July and aims to create awareness about tiger conservation. This sentence expands on the topic introduced in sentence C and adds another important detail about the day.

• Sentence B follows and states the primary objective of preserving the natural habitat of the tiger. This sentence is important because it highlights the main purpose of tiger conservation efforts, which is to ensure that tigers have a safe and secure natural environment to live in.

• Finally, sentence A provides additional detail by mentioning that while India is home to 75% of tigers in the world, neighboring countries like Bangladesh and Nepal also organize awareness events on this day. This sentence provides a geographical context for the day and emphasizes that tiger conservation is a global issue.

• Overall, the correct sequence of the sentences (CDBA) forms a coherent paragraph that introduces the topic of International Tiger Day, explains its objectives and importance, and provides additional details about tiger conservation efforts around the world.

Correct Sequence: *International Tiger Day was initiated in 2010, at the Saint Petersburg Tiger Summit. This annual event, observed on 29 July, aims to create awareness on tiger conservation. Its primary objective is to preserve the natural habitat of the tiger. While India is home to 75 per cent of tigers in the world, the Global Tiger Day - as it is also known - sees awareness events organised in the country, as well as neighbouring Bangladesh and Nepal.*

questions.q:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.

Words that begin with the same letter, syllable or sound
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'Alliteration'.

Key Points

• The most appropriate word for the given group of words is 'Alliteration'.

• Alliteration - समानाधिकारी (samaanaadhikaari)

• Meaning in English: The occurrence of the same letter or sound at the beginning of adjacent or closely connected words.

• *Example: Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers. This sentence uses alliteration by repeating the "p" sound at the beginning of several words.*

Correct Answer: *Alliteration.*

Additional Information

• Let's look at the meaning of other words:

questions.solution:

Key Points

• The most appropriate word for the given blank is 'hotel'.

• The sentence implies that the journalists are waiting in an entrance hall or open area of a public building, where they are likely to be waiting for someone or something.

• Therefore, the most appropriate option is "hotel", as hotels often have large, spacious lobbies or foyers where guests can wait for check-in or other activities.

• *Example: She walked into the hotel foyer to find a gaggle of tourists waiting for their tour bus.*

Correct Sentence: *A gaggle of journalists sit in a hotel foyer waiting impatiently.*
